claim: mib1 morphants display impaired Convergence Extension (CE) movements during zebrafish gastrulation.
source: mib1 null mutants and morphants display impaired Convergence Extension (CE) movements.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced axis extension in mib1 morphants (Figure 1A) and widening of notochord, somites, and neural plate (Figure 1B).

claim: The mib1 exon/intron1 splice site morpholino has been previously validated in different studies.
source: The mib1 exon/intron1 splice site morpholino used in these experiments has been previously validated in different studies (Itoh et al., 2003; Sharma et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior validation studies.

claim: Co-injection of wild-type mib1 RNA that is not targetable by the morpholino restores axis extension in mib1 morphants.
source: We further confirmed its specificity by showing that the co-injection of a WT mib1 RNA that is not targetable by the morpholino restores axis extension (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental rescue data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: mib1 morphants present a widening of the notochord, somites, and neural plate.
source: mib1 morphants present a widening of the notochord, somites, and neural plate. Dorsal views of 2 somite stage embryos, anterior up. dlx3 in situ hybridization outlines the neural plate, papc the somites and the adaxial cells lining the notochord.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data and measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The mib1ta52b mutation has no effect on axis extension.
source: In spite of the strong, antimorphic Notch loss-of-function phenotypes observed in mib1ta52b mutants, axial extension occurs normally in these animals (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing normal axis extension in mib1ta52b mutants.

claim: The mib1ta52b mutation disrupts the ability of Mib1 to promote Delta ubiquitination.
source: The mib1ta52b mutation in the C-terminal Mib1 RING finger domain (RF3, Figure 1C) disrupts the ability of the protein to promote Delta ubiquitination (Itoh et al., 2003; Sharma et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2007a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies demonstrating loss of ubiquitination activity.

claim: The Mib1ta52b mutant protein retains the ability to bind Delta ligands.
source: The Mib1ta52b mutant protein retains however the ability to bind Delta ligands (Itoh et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2007a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies showing retained binding activity.

claim: Mib1ta52b exerts a dominant-negative activity that leads to stronger Notch loss of function phenotypes in mib1ta52b point mutants compared to mib1tfi91 null mutants.
source: Through this ability to sequester Delta in an enzymatically inactive complex, Mib1ta52b exerts a dominant-negative activity that leads to the appearance of stronger Notch loss of function phenotypes in mib1ta52b point mutants compared to mib1tfi91 null mutants (Mikami et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2007b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies demonstrating dominant-negative effects.

claim: Constitutively activated Notch (NICD) fails to rescue mib1 morphant axis extension.
source: In accordance with this hypothesis, a constitutively activated form of Notch (NICD) that is able to restore Notch-dependent defects in the nervous system (Sharma et al., 2019) fails to rescue mib1 morphant axis extension (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing lack of rescue by NICD.

claim: The mib1 morpholino causes retention of intron1 leading to a premature Stop codon.
source: Sequencing of the mib1 cDNA in mib1 morphants revealed a retention of intron1 that causes the appearance of a premature Stop codon (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The Mib1 morphant protein comprises only the first 76 amino acids of WT Mib1.
source: As a consequence, the Mib1 morphant protein comprises only the first 76 amino acids of WT Mib1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Inferred from sequencing data showing premature stop codon.

claim: mib1 WT and mib1ta52b mutant RNAs are equally capable of rescuing mib1 morphant CE phenotypes.
source: Accordingly, mib1 WT and mib1ta52b mutant RNAs are equally capable of rescuing mib1 morphant CE phenotypes (Figure 1A and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental rescue data shown in Figures 1A, 1F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: mib1tfi91 homozygous animals present CE defects that are statistically significant, although weaker than in mib1 morphants.
source: In contrast to mib1ta52b mutants, mib1tfi91 homozygous animals present CE defects that are statistically significant, although weaker than in mib1 morphants (Figure 1G and H, Cohen's d effect size = 0.49 for mib1tfi91, 1.23 for MO mib1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis showing effect sizes.

claim: Similar CE phenotypes are observed for the mib1nce2a allele.
source: Similar phenotypes are observed for a new potential null allele generated in the present study (mib1nce2a, Figure 1C and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, F) or in mib1tfi91/nce2a trans-heterozygotes (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, 1G, and supplementary figures.

claim: mib1 transcript levels appear reduced in mib1tfi91 and mib1nce2a but not in mib1ta52b mutants.
source: Accordingly, mib1 transcript levels appear reduced in mib1tfi91 and mib1nce2a but not in mib1ta52b mutants (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, D,E).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and qPCR data shown in figures.

claim: Zebrafish Mib1 interacts with Epb41l5 to regulate neuronal differentiation.
source: Zebrafish Mib1 interacts with Epb41l5 to regulate neuronal differentiation (Matsuda et al., 2016) and with Catenin delta1 to control cell migration (Mizoguchi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Zebrafish Mib1 interacts with Catenin delta1 to control cell migration.
source: Zebrafish Mib1 interacts with Epb41l5 to regulate neuronal differentiation (Matsuda et al., 2016) and with Catenin delta1 to control cell migration (Mizoguchi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Both Mib1-Epb41l5 and Mib1-Catenin delta1 interactions are disrupted in mib1ta52b mutants.
source: Both of these activities are disrupted in mib1ta52b mutants (Matsuda et al., 2016; Mizoguchi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Vertebrate CE requires non-canonical Wnt/PCP signaling.
source: Vertebrate CE requires non-canonical Wnt/PCP signaling (Butler and Wallingford, 2017; Davey and Moens, 2017; Gray et al., 2011; Tada and Heisenberg, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: RhoA overexpression fully restores axis extension in mib1 morphants.
source: RhoA fully restores axis extension (Figure 2A), suggesting thereby that Mib1 is required for the PCP-dependent control of embryonic CE movements.
evidence: Supported by experimental rescue data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mib1 is required for the PCP-dependent control of embryonic CE movements.
source: RhoA fully restores axis extension (Figure 2A), suggesting thereby that Mib1 is required for the PCP-dependent control of embryonic CE movements.
evidence: Inferred from RhoA rescue experiment.

claim: All Mib1 functions known to date require its E3 ubiquitin ligase activity that is dependent on the presence of C-terminal RING finger domains.
source: All Mib1 functions known to date require its E3 ubiquitin ligase activity that is dependent of the presence of C-terminal RING finger domains (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior review.

claim: The N-terminal part of Mib1 is responsible for the interaction of Mib1 with different substrates.
source: In contrast, the N-terminal part of the protein is responsible for the interaction of Mib1 with different substrates (Berndt et al., 2011; Itoh et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2007a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mib1ΔRF123 enhances the defects of mib1 morphants and impairs axis extension in WT animals.
source: Similarly, a truncated Mib1 variant that lacks all three RING Finger domains (Mib1ΔRF123, Figure 1C) enhances the defects of mib1 morphants as well as impairing axis extension in WT animals (Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A Mib1 variant lacking only the last RING finger (Mib1ΔRF3) produces similar results to Mib1ΔRF123.
source: A Mib1 variant lacking only the last RING finger (Mib1ΔRF3, Figure 1C) produced similar results (Figure 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mammalian Mib1 controls the ubiquitin-dependent endocytic internalization of Ryk.
source: Mammalian Mib1 has been shown to control the ubiquitin-dependent endocytic internalization of the the Wnt co-receptor Receptor like tyrosine kinase Ryk (Berndt et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Studies in mice, frogs and zebrafish have implicated Ryk in non-canonical Wnt/PCP signaling.
source: Interestingly, studies in mice, frogs and zebrafish have implicated Ryk in non-canonical Wnt/PCP signaling (Kim et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2010; Macheda et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Ryk localizes to the cell surface as well as intracellular compartments.
source: Ryk localizes to the cell surface as well as intracellular compartments (Figure 3A), 70.7% of which are positive for the early endosomal marker Rab5 (n = 75 cells from eight embryos, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Berndt et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 70.7% of Ryk-positive intracellular compartments are positive for the early endosomal marker Rab5.
source: Ryk localizes to the cell surface as well as intracellular compartments (Figure 3A), 70.7% of which are positive for the early endosomal marker Rab5 (n = 75 cells from eight embryos, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Berndt et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by quantitative colocalization data from 75 cells.

claim: Mib1 overexpression depletes Ryk from the cell cortex and triggers its accumulation in intracellular compartments.
source: In accordance with a role of Mib1 in promoting Ryk endocytosis, Mib1 overexpression depleted Ryk from the cell cortex and triggered its accumulation in intracellular compartments (Figure 3B) without affecting the localization of the general plasma membrane marker GAP43-RFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Mib1 overexpression does not affect the localization of the general plasma membrane marker GAP43-RFP.
source: In accordance with a role of Mib1 in promoting Ryk endocytosis, Mib1 overexpression depleted Ryk from the cell cortex and triggered its accumulation in intracellular compartments (Figure 3B) without affecting the localization of the general plasma membrane marker GAP43-RFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Mibta52b misexpression promotes a relocalization of Ryk from the plasma membrane toward intracellular compartments.
source: In accordance with this hypothesis, Mibta52b misexpression promotes a relocalization of Ryk from the plasma membrane toward intracellular compartments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B), similar to the effect observed upon overexpression of wild-type Mib1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: Mib1 overexpression has no obvious effect on Vangl2 localization.
source: In contrast to Ryk, Mib1 overexpression has no obvious effect on Vangl2 localization (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Mib1 overexpression has no impact on the localization of Fz2 and Fz7.
source: Similarly, we detected no impact of Mib1 overexpression on the localization of Fz2 and Fz7, two Wnt receptors that have been in implicated in PCP signaling (Kim et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2010; Capek et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-D.

claim: Mib1 overexpression has no effect on the localization of zebrafish ROR2 or its orthologue ROR1.
source: Our experiments failed to identify an effect of Mib1 overexpression on the localization of zebrafish ROR2 or its orthologue ROR1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E-H).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E-H.

claim: Mib1 regulates CE movements through the specific control of Ryk localization.
source: Taken together, our observations suggest that Mib1 regulates CE movements through the specific control of Ryk localization.
evidence: Inferred from specificity experiments showing Mib1 affects Ryk but not other PCP proteins.

claim: mib1 morphants show a reduction in the number of RYK-GFP positive endosomes.
source: These experiments revealed a reduction in the number of Ryk-GFP positive endosomes in mib1 morphants (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative endosome counting data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Increasing the amount of injected Ryk-GFP RNA from 3 to 12 pg restores the number of Ryk positive endosomes in mib1 morphants.
source: Accordingly, increasing the amount of injected Ryk-GFP RNA from 3 to 12 pg restores the number of Ryk positive endosomes in mib1 morphants (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, B.

claim: High dose of Ryk-GFP fails to restore endosome number in embryos co-injected with mib1 morpholino and dominant-negative Mib1ΔRF123.
source: Even a high dose of Ryk-GFP fails, however, to restore endosome number in embryos co-injected with mib1 morpholino and dominant-negative Mib1ΔRF123 (Figure 3E, F and G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C, D), suggesting that Ryk can no more be internalized once Mib1 function is severely compromised.
evidence: Supported by quantitative endosome counting data shown in Figure 3E, F, G and Figure 3—figure supplement 4C, D.

claim: mib1tfi91 null mutants present a reduction in the number of RYK-GFP-positive endosomes.
source: Similar to mib1 morphants, mib1tfi91 null mutants present a reduction in the number of RYK-GFP-positive endosomes (Figure 3H, J, Figure 3—figure supplement 4E, F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative endosome counting data shown in Figure 3H, J and Figure 3—figure supplement 4E, F.

claim: Morphant and mutant embryos present a comparable reduction of the number of RYK-GFP-positive endosomes.
source: While stronger CE defects are observed in mib1 morphants compared to mib1 mutants (Figure 1G), morphant and mutant embryos present a comparable reduction of the number of RYK-GFP-positive endosomes (Figure 3J, Cohen's d effect size = 3.02 for mib1tfi91, 2.99 for mib1 morphants).
evidence: Supported by quantitative comparison with effect size analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: There exists a compensatory mechanism that allows to partially correct the PCP signaling defects that arise from a defect in Ryk endocytosis.
source: These observations suggest the existence of a compensatory mechanism that allows to partially correct the PCP signaling defects that arise from a defect in Ryk endocytosis.
evidence: Inferred from discrepancy between similar endosome reduction but different CE phenotype severity.

claim: In C. elegans, Mib1 controls Ryk cell surface levels by promoting Ryk internalization and degradation.
source: In C. elegans, Mib1 controls Ryk cell surface levels by promoting Ryk internalization and degradation (Berndt et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Zebrafish embryos injected with a high level of Mib1 RNA present an overall loss of Ryk-GFP signal.
source: Similarly, zebrafish embryos injected with a high level of Mib1 RNA present an overall loss of Ryk-GFP signal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) that can also be observed upon misexpression of the Mib1ta52b mutant protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Ryk-GFP overexpression restores axis extension in mib1 morphants.
source: In accordance with this later hypothesis, Ryk-GFP overexpression restores axis extension in mib1 morphants (Figure 3K) and mib1tfi91 mutants (Figure 3L).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3K and 3L.

claim: Ryk-GFP overexpression restores axis extension in mib1tfi91 mutants.
source: In accordance with this later hypothesis, Ryk-GFP overexpression restores axis extension in mib1 morphants (Figure 3K) and mib1tfi91 mutants (Figure 3L).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3K and 3L.

claim: Vangl2 overexpression did not display rescuing activity in mib1 morphants.
source: In contrast, Vangl2 overexpression did not display rescuing activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Co-injection of mib1 and ryk morpholinos causes CE defects that are significantly enhanced compared to single morphants.
source: Co-injection of mib1 and ryk morpholinos causes CE defects that are significantly enhanced compared to single morphants (Figure 3M), adding further support to our hypothesis that the CE defect of Mib1-depleted embryos are due to Ryk loss of function.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing enhanced phenotypes in double morphants shown in Figure 3M.

claim: The injection of morpholino-insensitive mib1 or ryk RNAs allows to rescue the CE defects that are generated by their respective morpholinos.
source: The injection of morpholino-insensitive mib1 or ryk RNAs allows to rescue the CE defects that are generated by their respective morpholinos, validating thereby the specificity of the reagents (Figure 1A and Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1A, Figure 4D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ryknce4g mutation introduces a premature stop codon that truncates the extracellular domain and deletes the transmembrane and cytoplasmic parts of the protein.
source: The ryknce4g mutation introduces a premature stop codon that truncates the extracellular domain and deletes the transmembrane and cytoplasmic parts of the protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by sequencing and protein structure analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The nce4g mutation abolishes the detection of an HA-tag located at C-terminus of the wild-type Ryk protein.
source: Accordingly, the nce4g mutation abolishes the detection of an HA-tag located at C-terminus of the wild-type protein (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: ryknce4g RNA fails to rescue ryk morphant CE defects.
source: In contrast to wild-type RNA, ryknce4g RNA fails to rescue ryk morphant CE defects (Figure 4D and E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4D, E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: High levels of WT ryk RNA induce severe embryonic malformations, while no overexpression phenotypes were observed using ryknce4g mutant RNA.
source: While high levels of WT ryk RNA induce severe embryonic malformations, no overexpression phenotypes were observed using ryknce4g mutant RNA (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by overexpression experiment data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Zygotic ryknce4g mutants show no CE defects.
source: Despite this evidence for functional ryk inactivation, our analysis failed to reveal CE defects in zygotic ryknce4g mutants (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ryk transcript levels are reduced in ryknce4g mutants.
source: Accordingly, ryk transcript levels are reduced in ryknce4g mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, G).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, G.

claim: Maternal Zygotic (MZ) ryknce4g mutants present highly significant CE defects compared to wild-type control animals from the same genetic background.
source: In contrast to zygotic mutants, Maternal Zygotic (MZ) ryknce4g mutants present highly significant CE defects compared to wild-type control animals from the same genetic background (Figure 4H–J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F, see methods for details).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H–J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: WT ryk RNA injection induces a significant rescue of CE in MZ ryknce4g mutants.
source: WT ryk RNA injection induces a significant rescue of CE, confirming thereby the specificity of the observed phenotypes (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: ryknce4g mutants are insensitive to the injection of a translation-blocking ryk morpholino.
source: In further accordance with a loss of ryk activity in these animals, ryknce4g mutants are insensitive to the injection of a translation-blocking ryk morpholino that can target both maternal and zygotic RNAs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by morpholino injection data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: MZ ryknce4g;mib1tfi91 double mutants display no significant difference in CE compared to MZ ryknce4g single mutants.
source: MZ ryknce4g;mib1tfi91 double mutants display no significant difference in CE compared to MZ ryknce4g single mutants (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Mib1 loss of function has no further consequences on CE in animals that are already devoid of Ryk.
source: This observation is in agreement with our model that the genetic inactivation of mib1 results in a specific impairment of Ryk activity. Accordingly, Mib1 loss of function has no further consequences on CE in animals that are already devoid of Ryk.
evidence: Inferred from double mutant analysis showing no additive effect.

claim: Ryk interacts with the PCP ligand Wnt5b to control gastrulation movements in zebrafish.
source: Previous work in zebrafish showed that Ryk interacts with the PCP ligand Wnt5b to control gastrulation movements (Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: A subliminal dose of Wnt5b morpholino that has no effect in wild-type controls is sufficient to significantly enhance the CE defects of mib1 morphants.
source: Our experiments show that the injection of a subliminal dose of Wnt5b morpholino that has no effect in wild-type controls is already sufficient to significantly enhance the CE defects of mib1 morphants (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: wnt5b morpholino injection impairs CE in mib1tfi91 WT siblings.
source: The existence of functional interactions between mib1 and wnt5b was further confirmed through wnt5b morpholino injections in mib1tfi91 mutants. Interestingly, the same dose of wnt5b morpholino that we showed to have no effect in ABTÜ wild-type controls (Figure 5A) not only decreased CE defects in mib1tfi91 homozygous mutants (Figure 5C), but also had a significant effect on CE in their WT siblings (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: wnt5b morpholino injection enhances CE defects in mib1tfi91 homozygous mutants.
source: Interestingly, the same dose of wnt5b morpholino that we showed to have no effect in ABTÜ wild-type controls (Figure 5A) not only decreased CE defects in mib1tfi91 homozygous mutants (Figure 5C), but also had a significant effect on CE in their WT siblings (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The reduction of mib1 gene dosage in mib1tfi91 WT siblings is sufficient to reveal the existence of genetic interactions between mib1 and wnt5b.
source: This later observation suggests that the reduction of mib1 gene dosage that is already present in these WT sibling embryos is already sufficient to reveal the existence of genetic interactions between mib1 and wnt5b.
evidence: Inferred from observation that wnt5b morpholino affects WT siblings of mib1 mutants.

claim: Through its ability to control Ryk localization, Mib1 may act as a modulator of Wnt5b-dependent CE movements.
source: In accordance with the previously reported function of Wnt5b/Ryk signaling in zebrafish gastrulation (Lin et al., 2010), our findings therefore suggest that through its ability to control Ryk localization, Mib1 may act as a modulator of Wnt5b-dependent CE movements.
evidence: Inferred from genetic interaction data and prior knowledge of Wnt5b/Ryk signaling.

claim: Overexpression of high amounts of Mib1 or Wnt5b cause an overall reduction of Ryk-GFP levels.
source: Our experiments reveal that overexpression of high amounts of Mib1 (125 pg, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) or Wnt5b (300 pg, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B) cause an overall reduction of Ryk-GFP levels, in accordance with the previously reported function of Mib1 in Ryk degradation (Berndt et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Wnt5b misexpression does not result in a clear relocalization of Ryk-GFP from the plasma membrane to intracellular compartments.
source: While the overexpression of lower amounts of Mib1 results in a clear relocalization of Ryk-GFP from the plasma membrane to intracellular compartments (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, E), we never observed a similar intracellular accumulation of Ryk upon Wnt5b misexpression.
evidence: Supported by imaging experiments comparing Mib1 and Wnt5b effects.

claim: The loss of Ryk-GFP expression observed upon overexpression of high amounts of Wnt5b does not require Mib1 function.
source: In accordance with this hypothesis, the loss of Ryk-GFP expression that is observed upon overexpression of high amounts of Wnt5b does not require Mib1 function (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in mib1 mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Mib1 is not involved in the Wnt5b-dependent control of Ryk localization.
source: The different effects of Wnt5b and Mib1 overexpression suggest that Mib1 is not involved in the Wnt5b-dependent control of Ryk localization.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of Wnt5b and Mib1 on Ryk localization.

claim: Through its ability to control endocytic Ryk internalization, Mib1 acts as an essential modulator of Ryk/Wnt5b-mediated PCP signaling.
source: Taken together our findings identify the E3 Ubiquitin ligase Mib1 as a novel regulator of PCP-dependent CE movements. While the precise cellular and molecular mechanism that underlies Mib1 function in PCP signaling remains to be established, we provide evidence that through its ability to control endocytic Ryk internalization, Mib1 acts as an essential modulator of Ryk/Wnt5b-mediated PCP signaling.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence showing Mib1 controls Ryk endocytosis and interacts genetically with Wnt5b.

claim: Notch signaling is severely impaired upon genetic inactivation or morpholino knock-down of mib1 in mice, Xenopus and zebrafish.
source: In contrast, Notch signaling is severely impaired upon genetic inactivation or morpholino knock-down of mib1 in mice, Xenopus and zebrafish (Itoh et al., 2003; Koo et al., 2007; Yoon et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mutational analysis in zebrafish failed to confirm a requirement for mib2 in Notch signaling.
source: Nonetheless, mutational analysis in zebrafish failed to confirm a requirement for mib2 in Notch signaling (Mikami et al., 2015) and showed that a mib1 inactivation is sufficient to essentially abolish the expression of a transgenic Notch reporter in the central nervous system (Sharma et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: mib1 inactivation is sufficient to essentially abolish the expression of a transgenic Notch reporter in the central nervous system.
source: Nonetheless, mutational analysis in zebrafish failed to confirm a requirement for mib2 in Notch signaling (Mikami et al., 2015) and showed that a mib1 inactivation is sufficient to essentially abolish the expression of a transgenic Notch reporter in the central nervous system (Sharma et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Mib1 is the major regulator of vertebrate DSL ligand endocytosis.
source: These findings identify Mib1 as the major regulator of vertebrate DSL ligand endocytosis.
evidence: Inferred from multiple studies showing Mib1 is essential for Notch signaling.

claim: Mib1 is able to interact with a number of additional substrate proteins beyond Delta ligands.
source: In addition to Delta ligands, Mib1 is able to interact with a number of additional substrate proteins (Berndt et al., 2011; Matsuda et al., 2016; Mertz et al., 2015; Tseng et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Functional studies have implicated Mib1 in the regulation of epithelial morphogenesis.
source: Accordingly, functional studies have implicated Mib1 in a growing number of functions that include the regulation of epithelial morphogenesis (Dho et al., 2019; Matsuda et al., 2016) and cell migration (Mizoguchi et al., 2017), centrosome and cilia biogenesis (Douanne et al., 2019; Joachim et al., 2017; Villumsen et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Cajanek et al., 2015), the control of glutamate receptor localization (Sturgeon et al., 2016) or interferon production (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Functional studies have implicated Mib1 in cell migration.
source: Accordingly, functional studies have implicated Mib1 in a growing number of functions that include the regulation of epithelial morphogenesis (Dho et al., 2019; Matsuda et al., 2016) and cell migration (Mizoguchi et al., 2017), centrosome and cilia biogenesis (Douanne et al., 2019; Joachim et al., 2017; Villumsen et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Cajanek et al., 2015), the control of glutamate receptor localization (Sturgeon et al., 2016) or interferon production (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Functional studies have implicated Mib1 in centrosome and cilia biogenesis.
source: Accordingly, functional studies have implicated Mib1 in a growing number of functions that include the regulation of epithelial morphogenesis (Dho et al., 2019; Matsuda et al., 2016) and cell migration (Mizoguchi et al., 2017), centrosome and cilia biogenesis (Douanne et al., 2019; Joachim et al., 2017; Villumsen et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Cajanek et al., 2015), the control of glutamate receptor localization (Sturgeon et al., 2016) or interferon production (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Functional studies have implicated Mib1 in the control of glutamate receptor localization.
source: Accordingly, functional studies have implicated Mib1 in a growing number of functions that include the regulation of epithelial morphogenesis (Dho et al., 2019; Matsuda et al., 2016) and cell migration (Mizoguchi et al., 2017), centrosome and cilia biogenesis (Douanne et al., 2019; Joachim et al., 2017; Villumsen et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Cajanek et al., 2015), the control of glutamate receptor localization (Sturgeon et al., 2016) or interferon production (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Functional studies have implicated Mib1 in interferon production.
source: Accordingly, functional studies have implicated Mib1 in a growing number of functions that include the regulation of epithelial morphogenesis (Dho et al., 2019; Matsuda et al., 2016) and cell migration (Mizoguchi et al., 2017), centrosome and cilia biogenesis (Douanne et al., 2019; Joachim et al., 2017; Villumsen et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Cajanek et al., 2015), the control of glutamate receptor localization (Sturgeon et al., 2016) or interferon production (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A study in human cell culture identified Ryk as a target of Mib1-mediated ubiquitination.
source: A study in human cell culture identified the Receptor-like tyrosine kinase Ryk as a target of Mib1-mediated ubiquitination (Berndt et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Ryk is a single-pass transmembrane protein that binds Wnt ligands through its extracellular Wnt Inhibitory Factor (WIF) domain.
source: Ryk is a single-pass transmembrane protein that binds Wnt ligands through its extracellular Wnt Inhibitory Factor (WIF) domain.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Ryk protein structure.

claim: Ryk's intracellular pseudokinase domain appears devoid of functional enzymatic activity.
source: While its intracellular pseudokinase domain appears devoid of functional enzymatic activity, Ryk has been suggested to regulate cell signaling through scaffolding functions or the γ-secretase-dependent release and nuclear translocation of its intracellular domain (Roy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior review.

claim: Ryk has been suggested to regulate cell signaling through scaffolding functions or the γ-secretase-dependent release and nuclear translocation of its intracellular domain.
source: While its intracellular pseudokinase domain appears devoid of functional enzymatic activity, Ryk has been suggested to regulate cell signaling through scaffolding functions or the γ-secretase-dependent release and nuclear translocation of its intracellular domain (Roy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior review.

claim: A number of studies have implicated Ryk in canonical, β-catenin-dependent Wnt signaling.
source: A number of studies have implicated Ryk in canonical, β-catenin-dependent Wnt signaling (Green et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2004; Roy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mib1 promotes the ubiquitination and internalization of Ryk, which appears to be required for Wnt3A-mediated β-catenin stabilization/activation.
source: In this context, Mib1 has been shown to promote the ubiquitination and internalization of Ryk, which appears to be required for Wnt3A-mediated β-catenin stabilization/activation (Berndt et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Experiments in C. elegans provided evidence for genetic interactions between mib1 and ryk.
source: While experiments in C. elegans provided evidence for genetic interactions between mib1 and ryk (Berndt et al., 2011), the importance of Mib1/Ryk interactions for vertebrate development or physiology has not been addressed.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Several studies have linked Ryk to the non-canonical, β-catenin independent, Wnt/Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) and Wnt/Ca2+ pathways.
source: In addition to its role in canonical Wnt signaling, several studies have linked Ryk to the non-canonical, β-catenin independent, Wnt/Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) and Wnt/Ca2+ pathways (Duan et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2010; Macheda et al., 2012; Roy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Ryk mutant mice present a range of diagnostic PCP phenotypes, including defects in neural tube closure and the orientation of inner ear sensory hair cells.
source: Ryk mutant mice present a range of diagnostic PCP phenotypes, including defects in neural tube closure and the orientation of inner ear sensory hair cells (Andre et al., 2012; Macheda et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: During early fish and frog development, PCP signaling regulates Wnt-dependent Convergent Extension (CE) movements that direct embryonic axis extension.
source: During early fish and frog development, PCP signaling regulates Wnt-dependent Convergent Extension (CE) movements that direct embryonic axis extension (Butler and Wallingford, 2017; Davey and Moens, 2017; Gray et al., 2011; Tada and Heisenberg, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior reviews and studies.

claim: Different studies have suggested that Ryk may control PCP by acting together with Wnt-binding Frizzled (Fz) receptors.
source: Different studies have suggested that Ryk may control PCP by acting together with Wnt-binding Frizzled (Fz) receptors (Kim et al., 2008), regulating a Fz-independent parallel pathway (Lin et al., 2010) or by controlling the stability of the core PCP pathway component Vangl2 (Andre et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Ryk may control PCP by regulating a Fz-independent parallel pathway.
source: Different studies have suggested that Ryk may control PCP by acting together with Wnt-binding Frizzled (Fz) receptors (Kim et al., 2008), regulating a Fz-independent parallel pathway (Lin et al., 2010) or by controlling the stability of the core PCP pathway component Vangl2 (Andre et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Ryk may control PCP by controlling the stability of the core PCP pathway component Vangl2.
source: Different studies have suggested that Ryk may control PCP by acting together with Wnt-binding Frizzled (Fz) receptors (Kim et al., 2008), regulating a Fz-independent parallel pathway (Lin et al., 2010) or by controlling the stability of the core PCP pathway component Vangl2 (Andre et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The core PCP machinery is defined by three transmembrane proteins Flamingo(Fmi)/CELSR, Fz and Strabismus/Vangl as well as their cytoplasmic partners Dishevelled (Dvl), Prickle (Pk) and Diego (Dgo)/ANKRD6.
source: In both vertebrates and invertebrates, the core PCP machinery is defined by three transmembrane proteins Flamingo(Fmi)/CELSR, Fz and Strabismus/Vangl as well as their cytoplasmic partners Dishevelled (Dvl), Prickle (Pk) and Diego (Dgo)/ANKRD6 (Butler and Wallingford, 2017; Devenport, 2014; Harrison et al., 2020; Humphries and Mlodzik, 2018; Vladar et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior reviews establishing core PCP components.

claim: Polarity is established through formation of distinct CELSR/Vangl/Pk and CELSR/Fz/Dvl/Dgo complexes at the opposite sides of the cell.
source: Polarity is established through formation of distinct CELSR/Vangl/Pk and CELSR/Fz/Dvl/Dgo complexes at the opposite sides of the cell.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PCP complex organization.

claim: The levels of individual PCP pathway components need to be tightly controlled.
source: The fact that similar defects are often observed upon overexpression or inactivation of PCP pathway components suggests that the levels of individual proteins need to be tightly controlled.
evidence: Inferred from observation that both overexpression and loss cause similar defects.

claim: Dynamin, Rab5 and other regulators of membrane trafficking control the distribution of the transmembrane proteins Fmi/CELSR, Fz and Vangl2.
source: It is therefore no surprise that factors such as Dynamin, which governs endocytic vesicle scission, the early endosomal GTPase Rab5 and other regulators of membrane trafficking have been shown to control the distribution of the transmembrane proteins Fmi/CELSR, Fz and Vangl2 (Butler and Wallingford, 2017; Devenport et al., 2011; Mottola et al., 2010; Strutt and Strutt, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Endocytosis ensures the PCP-dependent regulation of cellular adhesion molecules.
source: In addition to regulating the trafficking of core pathway components, endocytosis ensures the PCP-dependent regulation of cellular adhesion molecules (Classen et al., 2005; Ulrich et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mib1 inactivation is often used to inhibit Notch signaling.
source: Mib1 inactivation is therefore often used to inhibit Notch signaling.
evidence: Based on established practice in the field.

claim: Recent findings indicate that Mib1 function extends beyond the Notch pathway.
source: However, recent findings indicate that Mib1 function extends beyond the Notch pathway.
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mib1 controls CE independently of Notch.
source: Comparison of different mib1 mutants and functional rescue experiments indicate that Mib1 controls CE independently of Notch.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental approaches including mutant analysis and rescue experiments.

claim: Mib1-dependent CE defects can be rescued using the Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) downstream mediator RhoA.
source: Mib1-dependent CE defects can be rescued using the Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) downstream mediator RhoA, or enhanced through knock-down of the PCP ligand Wnt5b.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mib1-dependent CE defects can be enhanced through knock-down of the PCP ligand Wnt5b.
source: Mib1-dependent CE defects can be rescued using the Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) downstream mediator RhoA, or enhanced through knock-down of the PCP ligand Wnt5b.
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mib1 regulates CE through its RING Finger domains that have been implicated in substrate ubiquitination.
source: Mib1 regulates CE through its RING Finger domains that have been implicated in substrate ubiquitination, suggesting that Mib1 may control PCP protein trafficking.
evidence: Supported by experiments with RING finger deletion mutants shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mib1 may control PCP protein trafficking.
source: Mib1 regulates CE through its RING Finger domains that have been implicated in substrate ubiquitination, suggesting that Mib1 may control PCP protein trafficking.
evidence: Inferred from requirement of RING finger domains and known role in ubiquitination.

claim: Mib1 controls the endocytosis of the PCP component Ryk.
source: Accordingly, we show that Mib1 controls the endocytosis of the PCP component Ryk and that Ryk internalization is required for CE.
evidence: Supported by endosome quantification data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ryk internalization is required for CE.
source: Accordingly, we show that Mib1 controls the endocytosis of the PCP component Ryk and that Ryk internalization is required for CE.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing Ryk overexpression restores CE in mib1 mutants.

claim: During zebrafish gastrulation Mib1 exerts a Notch-independent control of PCP-dependent CE movements.
source: Our observation that during zebrafish gastrulation Mib1 exerts a Notch-independent control of PCP-dependent CE movements suggest that Mib1 loss-of-function phenotypes should be cautiously interpreted depending on the biological context.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence throughout the study.

claim: Mib1 loss-of-function phenotypes should be cautiously interpreted depending on the biological context.
source: Our observation that during zebrafish gastrulation Mib1 exerts a Notch-independent control of PCP-dependent CE movements suggest that Mib1 loss-of-function phenotypes should be cautiously interpreted depending on the biological context.
evidence: Inferred from discovery of Notch-independent Mib1 function.

claim: Numerous morphogenetic processes involve both Notch and PCP signaling.
source: Numerous morphogenetic processes involve both Notch and PCP signaling.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: Endocytic membrane trafficking is essential to control the abundance, localization, and activity of cellular signaling molecules.
source: Endocytic membrane trafficking is essential to control the abundance, localization, and activity of cellular signaling molecules.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: Delta ligand endocytosis is required for Notch receptor activation.
source: One key example for the importance of endosomal membrane trafficking is provided by the Delta/Notch signaling pathway, where Delta ligand endocytosis is required for Notch receptor activation (Chitnis, 2006; Fürthauer and González-Gaitán, 2009; Le Borgne et al., 2005a; Seib and Klein, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior reviews.

claim: Productive ligand/receptor interactions trigger a series of proteolytic cleavages that release the Notch Intracellular Domain (NICD) into the cytoplasm.
source: Productive ligand/receptor interactions trigger a series of proteolytic cleavages that release the Notch Intracellular Domain (NICD) into the cytoplasm, allowing it to enter the nucleus and associate with transcriptional cofactors to activate target gene expression.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Notch signaling mechanism.

claim: Ubiquitin-dependent endocytosis of DSL ligands in signal-sending cells is essential to promote Notch receptor activation in adjacent signal-receiving cells.
source: Studies in Drosophila and vertebrates revealed that Ubiquitin-dependent endocytosis of DSL ligands in signal-sending cells is essential to promote Notch receptor activation in adjacent signal-receiving cells (Deblandre et al., 2001; Itoh et al., 2003; Lai et al., 2001; Le Borgne and Schweisguth, 2003; Pavlopoulos et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Current models suggest that the endocytosis of DSL ligands represents a force-generating event that physically pulls on Notch receptors to promote their activation.
source: While the precise mechanism through which Delta promotes Notch activation is still under investigation, current models suggest that the endocytosis of DSL ligands represents a force-generating event that physically pulls on Notch receptors to promote their activation (Langridge and Struhl, 2017; Meloty-Kapella et al., 2012; Seib and Klein, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies proposing mechanical pulling model.

claim: Notch pathway activation is critically dependent on Delta endocytosis, a process controlled by ligand polyubiquitination.
source: Notch pathway activation is therefore critically dependent on Delta endocytosis, a process controlled by ligand polyubiquitination.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Notch signaling mechanism.

claim: Protein ubiquitination involves ubiquitin-activating E1 enzymes, ubiquitin-conjugating E2 enzymes and substrate-specific E3 ubiquitin ligases.
source: Protein ubiquitination involves ubiquitin-activating E1 enzymes, ubiquitin-conjugating E2 enzymes and substrate-specific E3 ubiquitin ligases (Oh et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ubiquitination machinery.

claim: Two different RING finger domain E3 ligases, Neuralized (Neur) and Mindbomb (Mib) control DSL ligand endocytosis in Drosophila.
source: Genetic studies revealed that two different RING (Really Interesting New Gene) finger domain E3 ligases, Neuralized (Neur) and Mindbomb (Mib) control DSL ligand endocytosis in Drosophila (Lai et al., 2001; Le Borgne et al., 2005b; Le Borgne and Schweisguth, 2003; Pavlopoulos et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior genetic studies.

claim: Vertebrate genomes harbor two mib and several neur homologues.
source: Vertebrate genomes harbor two mib and several neur homologues.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of vertebrate genome organization.

claim: Mouse neur1 or neur2 single and double mutants present no phenotypes indicative of defective Notch signaling.
source: However, mouse neur1 or neur2 single and double mutants present no phenotypes indicative of defective Notch signaling (Koo et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.
